summary:
This project develops a multimodal system for behavioral telemetry and the early detection of stress and fatigue, designed for isolated, confined, and extreme (ICE) environments, such as specialized laboratories and space missions. Utilizing an Edge AI architecture—executed via parallel multiprocessing without reliance on external servers—the software analyzes video in real time, ensuring visual privacy and minimal response latency.

The operational core integrates two branches, both synchronized at a 20 Hz sampling rate. The spatial branch combines YOLOv11-Pose and ByteTrack to track multiple individuals, assess ergonomic posture, monitor manual agitation, and identify self-regulatory gestures associated with anxiety; it also employs YOLO-World and CLIP to recognize 100 everyday and laboratory-specific objects, while timing their active manipulation. In parallel, the facial branch uses MediaPipe Face Landmarker to extract 478 3D landmarks and 52 FACS (Facial Action Coding System) muscle coefficients. These data are used to perform a 15-second individual baseline calibration, which normalizes facial tension via Z-scores while simultaneously quantifying brief micro-expressions (30–220 ms), blink frequency, drowsiness (PERCLOS), and gaze direction. Finally, an LSTM (Long Short-Term Memory) recurrent neural network classifies temporal sequences of cognitive load and stress, generating anonymized records in CSV format alongside graphical reports.
details:
1. Problem Statement and Theoretical Justification

Long-duration space missions and operations in isolated, confined, and extreme (ICE) environments expose crews to cumulative stressors: physical confinement, sensory monotony, circadian disruption, cognitive overload, chronic exposure to elevated carbon dioxide levels, and—in missions beyond low Earth orbit (LEO)—communication latencies that preclude real-time psychological support from Earth.

In aerospace medicine, the monitoring of Behavioral Health and Performance (BHP) faces a critical obstacle known as "psychological closing": highly trained crew members tend to minimize or mask symptoms of anxiety, exhaustion, or interpersonal conflict when responding to subjective questionnaires, in order to avoid compromising their operational status or alarming mission control.

To overcome self-reporting bias without resorting to invasive body-worn sensors that might interfere with operational tasks, this project bases its architecture on four theoretical pillars validated by psychophysiology and cognitive ergonomics:

Facial Action Coding System (FACS) and Micro-expression Dynamics: Drawing on the work of Ekman and Friesen, the involuntary activation of the sympathetic nervous system in response to a threat or cognitive overload triggers brief muscle micro-contractions (lasting 30 ms to 220 ms)—occurring before cortical control can inhibit them. The continuous measurement of specific "action units"—such as brow lowering (AU4/browDown), lip pressing (mouthPress), jaw clenching (jawClench), and eye squinting (eyeSquint)—provides an objective marker of covert emotional tension. Ocular Biomarkers of Fatigue and Cognitive Load: Spontaneous blink rate (BPM) is modulated by central dopaminergic activity and attentional demand; both abrupt blink suppression (hyper-concentration under acute stress) and erratic increases in blinking indicate cognitive dysregulation. Complementarily, the PERCLOS (Percentage of Eyelid Closure over the Pupil over Time) metric serves as the gold standard in human factors engineering for quantifying physiological drowsiness and detecting microsleeps that precede human error.

Non-Verbal Kinematics and Self-Regulatory Behaviors: In states of sustained anxiety, individuals perform unconscious, self-directed adaptive gestures (such as touching the face or rubbing the neck or head) and exhibit variations in motor agitation or postural rigidity ("freezing"). Geometric analysis of skeletal joints allows for the quantification of these behaviors without requiring input from the subject.

Human-Instrument Operational Contextualization: An isolated physiological indicator lacks diagnostic value unless linked to the task being performed. Correlating a subject's psychophysiological state with their active manipulation of everyday objects or technical laboratory equipment makes it possible to distinguish between productive cognitive effort and performance degradation during critical procedures.

2. Technological Architecture of the Proposed System

The system implements an Edge AI architecture, utilizing parallel processes managed via non-blocking shared-memory queues (zero-latency multiprocessing). This ensures real-time, local processing without any dependency on external servers:

Branch A — Spatial Perception, Body Kinematics, and Operational Context:

This branch integrates YOLOv11-pose with the ByteTrack multi-object tracker to extract 17 skeletal keypoints per individual, maintaining consistent identities across shared spaces. It incorporates an open-vocabulary detector based on YOLO-World, utilizing precomputed CLIP text embeddings (covering 100 classes: 50 everyday objects and 50 laboratory/controlled-environment instruments). This system calculates hand-object proximity, cumulative usage duration, postural ergonomics, and self-regulatory gestures associated with anxiety.

A geometric facial-exclusion filter is applied, preventing detection bounding boxes from overlapping with the facial area, thereby preserving optical integrity for biometric analysis.

Branch B — High-Frequency Facial Dynamics and Ocular Biomarkers:

MediaPipe Face Landmarker is employed to extract 478 3D facial landmarks, 52 expression coefficients (FACS blendshapes), and head-pose transformation matrices (yaw, pitch, and roll).

An intra-subject baseline calibration module records the resting state of each crew member to determine their individual mean and standard deviation , subsequently evaluating deviations via Z-scores.

It simultaneously calculates blink rate (BPM) and a drowsiness index.
